recent_posts.title: Functional Programming of Balls
recent_posts.summary: A live coding session exploring the use of Standard ML (SML) as a build system replacement for Makefiles in a raylib bindings project. The author uses Moscow ML to write a build script in SML that runs external commands via the process module, handles exit codes, implements string quoting for arguments, and ultimately replaces the Makefile entirely. Along the way, various SML quirks are discovered including module loading, pipe operator behavior, exception handling, and the ability to compile SML files from within the REPL itself.

recent_posts.title: Bindings Generator
recent_posts.summary: A live coding session building a deterministic bindings generator for Moscow ML (Standard ML) targeting the raylib C library. The author modifies raylib's existing C parser tool to output SML bindings instead of JSON/XML, implementing C-to-SML type mappings, handling FFI constraints like the 5-argument limit, generating both the SML signature file and the corresponding C wrapper file. Key challenges include translating C types to SML equivalents, handling pointers, dealing with ML's 31-bit integer quirk, and using GNU nested functions as a local helper. The session contrasts this deterministic approach against using LLMs for boilerplate generation.

recent_posts.title: Exploring Standard ML with Moscow ML implementation
recent_posts.summary: A live coding session exploring Standard ML, a functional programming language last standardized in 1997. The host attempts to build and run two implementations: SML/NJ (Standard ML of New Jersey) and Moscow ML. SML/NJ fails due to a missing gold linker dependency, while Moscow ML successfully compiles after patching C89 compatibility issues. The session covers installing Moscow ML, using its REPL, basic syntax (factorial, arrays, tuples, type inference), integrating with Emacs via an SML mode, and observations about the language's similarities to OCaml and its practical, non-dogmatic approach to functional programming compared to Haskell.

recent_posts.title: Reference Counting in C
recent_posts.summary: A live coding session implementing reference counting from scratch in C, motivated by the fact that C lacks built-in memory management. The session covers the theory of reference counting (incrementing/decrementing a counter per reference, freeing when count hits zero), its limitations like cyclic references and weak pointers, and a practical application: building a minimal Lisp/S-expression interpreter in C. The code constructs a tagged union for expression types (nil, symbol, integer, pair), builds list constructors with variadic macros, implements a basic evaluator for addition, and demonstrates memory leaks via Valgrind — setting up the motivation for adding reference counting to the allocator. The RC design allocates a counter header before the data payload, with acquire/release operations.

recent_posts.title: Very Big Integers
recent_posts.summary: A live coding session exploring arbitrary-precision (big integer) arithmetic in C, starting by implementing a custom big integer addition from scratch using dynamic arrays and carry-over logic, then comparing results against Python's built-in arbitrary precision integers. The second half covers downloading, building, and exploring the GNU Multiple Precision Arithmetic Library (GMP), including its header structure, MPZ integer type, and basic usage patterns discovered by reading source code and demos due to unavailable online documentation.

recent_posts.title: Collision Detection in C
recent_posts.summary: A live coding session implementing collision detection in C for a custom game engine. Covers the math behind sphere-box and rectangle-circle intersection using the closest-point technique (clamping center coordinates with min/max), then extends it to 3D. Also introduces a voxel-based barrier system using a hash set, adds a new 'barrier' entity kind to the game's entity system, computes axis-aligned bounding boxes from model vertices at asset-build time, and derives a rect-rect collision check by testing segment non-overlap per axis and negating.

recent_posts.title: Raylib from Jai
recent_posts.summary: A live coding session demonstrating how to use Raylib from the Jai programming language. Covers setting up foreign function bindings manually, using Jai's built-in bindings generator to auto-generate Raylib wrappers from C headers, structuring the generated code as a Jai module, handling library linking (including the math library), and running Raylib at both compile time and runtime. The session ends with starting a pendulum physics simulation using the generated bindings.
